questions.q: Why does the board's mandate specifically call for a zero-trust pilot rather than an enterprise-wide rollout?
options: Because zero trust only works on small networks
Because attempting identity, network, device, and data controls everywhere at once in 90 days on a fixed budget would produce something shallow everywhere instead of something real anywhere
Because the board didn't actually approve any budget for zero trust
Because a pilot requires no planning at all
questions.explain: A credible zero-trust program sequences a multi-year rollout; a pilot proves the model works on a real boundary first, which is what the 90-day, $340,000 Phase 1 budget can actually deliver.

questions.q: What specifically made Riverbend's OT/SCADA boundary the chosen pilot target over the corporate end-user network or SaaS access?
options: It was the cheapest boundary to fix
It has the highest blast radius of any Hartwell boundary and today sits on the same flat network as corporate IT with minimal containment
It was the only boundary Howard Okonjo had ever heard of
Corporate IT and SaaS access were already fully zero-trust
questions.explain: Riverbend's SCADA systems for a substation and water treatment sit on the same flat network as general corporate traffic, with only a single perimeter rule set standing between them — the highest-stakes, least-contained boundary at Hartwell.

questions.q: What four items are explicitly in scope for this 90-day pilot?
options: A new SIEM purchase, employee training, a vendor audit, and a password reset policy
Network segmentation of the Riverbend OT/SCADA boundary, a consolidated identity view of who can reach it, an automated Python inventory of that access, and a risk-register entry for every finding
Zero-trust access for every employee, a full identity governance audit, and a multi-site rollout
Only the network segmentation piece — identity and automation are out of scope entirely
questions.explain: The scope statement covers segmentation of the Riverbend boundary, the identity view scoped to that boundary's access, the Python-based automated inventory, and a risk-register entry per finding.

questions.q: Why does the scope document explicitly list what's deferred, not just what's included?
options: It's a formality with no real purpose
It gives Okonjo a defensible answer to the board's likely question of why everything wasn't fixed at once, framing the deferral as a decision rather than a gap
Deferred items are legally required to be listed
It's only there to make the document look longer
questions.explain: Writing down what's deferred — like enterprise-wide ZTNA or a full identity audit — lets the CISO explain to the board that the pilot's narrow scope was deliberate, with a stated plan for what comes next.

questions.q: What three questions did Mara and Okonjo use to evaluate candidate boundaries for the pilot?
options: Cost, popularity, and vendor support
Blast radius if the boundary fails, how contained it is today, and whether it can realistically be finished in 90 days
Which boundary had the most existing documentation
Which team complained about it most recently
questions.explain: The evaluation weighed blast radius, current containment, and 90-day feasibility — the combination that made Riverbend's OT/SCADA boundary the clear choice.
